procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 06.04.2023 passed in Criminal Revision Petition No.674/2022 by the High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The respondent (husband) filed an application under Section 25 of an unspecified Act. The Magistrate's order (dated 23-02-2015) in Crl. Mis. 6/2014 was challenged. The Appellate Court directed the Magistrate to consider the application under Section 25. The wife then filed Criminal Revision Petition No.674/2022 before the High Court, which dismissed the petition on 06.04.2023, directing the Magistrate to consider the Section 25 application without being influenced by the Appellate Court's observations in Criminal Appeal No.757/2020.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant (wife), being aggrieved by the High Court's order dated 06.04.2023 in Criminal Revision Petition No.674/2022, filed a Criminal Appeal (No. 3989 of 2024) before the Supreme Court, seeking to set aside the order dated 23-02-2015 passed in Crl. Mis. 6/2014.

issue.issue_text: Whether the power under Section 25(2) of the Act to alter, modify, or revoke a maintenance order can be exercised retrospectively to set aside an order that has attained finality for a period prior to the filing of the application.

facts: A maintenance order was passed on 23.02.2015, which had attained finality after an appeal against it was dismissed.
The respondent later filed an application under Section 25(2) of the Act.
The respondent's application sought to set aside the 23.02.2015 order and demanded a refund of all maintenance amounts already paid pursuant to that order.
law: Section 25(2) of the Act allows a Magistrate to alter, modify, or revoke a maintenance order if there is a 'change in the circumstances' that occurred *after* the original order was passed.

The power under Section 25(2) operates prospectively, not retrospectively. Any alteration, modification, or revocation takes effect from a future date, such as the date of the application for modification, but not for a period prior to it.

The court drew an analogy to Sections 125 and 127 of the CrPC, noting that while an initial maintenance order can be granted from the date of the application, the power to alter it (under Section 127 CrPC, similar to Section 25(2) of the Act) does not have a similar retrospective provision.
application: The Court found that the respondent was not seeking a modification based on a change in circumstances that occurred after the 2015 order. Instead, the respondent was attempting to set aside the original order itself, which had already become final.

The Court determined that the prayer for a refund of maintenance already paid was 'not at all maintainable'. This is because any modification under Section 25(2) can only apply 'ex post facto' (after the fact), meaning it can only affect the maintenance obligation from the date of the modification application onwards, not nullify past payments.

The Court concluded that using Section 25(2) to set aside a final order for a period before the application was filed is contrary to the spirit of the law. It cannot be used as a backdoor to challenge an order that was not properly appealed.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the retrospective use of Section 25(2), holding that the power to alter, modify, or revoke a maintenance order can only be exercised prospectively based on a change in circumstances arising after the original order. It cannot be used to set aside a final order for a period prior to the filing of the modification application or to claim a refund of maintenance already paid under that order.

issue.issue_text: Whether an application under Section 25(2) of the Act can be used to seek a refund of the maintenance amount already paid under the original order.

facts: A maintenance order was passed on 23.02.2015, which attained finality after an appeal against it was dismissed.
The respondent later filed an application under Section 25(2) of the Protection of Woman from Domestic Violence Act, 2005.

In this application, the respondent sought to revoke the original maintenance order and requested a refund of the entire amount of maintenance that had already been paid to the appellant pursuant to that order.
law: Section 25(2) of the Act allows a Magistrate to alter, modify, or revoke any order made under the Act.
To invoke Section 25(2), there must be a "change in the circumstances" that has occurred *after* the original order was passed.
Any alteration, modification, or revocation of an order under Section 25(2) operates prospectively, not retrospectively. It applies for a period *ex post facto* (after the original order was made).

The Court drew an analogy to Sections 125 and 127 of the CrPC, noting that while an initial maintenance order can be granted from the date of the application, the power to alter it under Section 127 does not have a similar retrospective provision.
application: The Supreme Court determined that the respondent's prayer for a refund of maintenance already paid was an attempt to apply the revocation of the order retrospectively.
The Court held that an application under Section 25(2) cannot relate to any period *prior* to the original order being passed or even prior to the filing of the application for modification.
Since the original maintenance order of 23.02.2015 had attained finality, it could not be set aside for the period before the application for revocation was made.

The Court found the prayer for a refund to be "not at all maintainable" and "totally contrary to the spirit" of Section 25(2), as the provision is meant to address future obligations based on changed circumstances, not to undo payments made under a valid and final past order.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that an application under Section 25(2) of the Act cannot be used to seek a refund of maintenance amounts already paid. Any alteration, modification, or revocation of a maintenance order under this section can only have prospective effect from the date of the application or as ordered by the Magistrate, and cannot be applied retrospectively to nullify past payments made under a final order.

issue.issue_text: Whether the jurisdiction of a Magistrate under Section 25(2) of the Act can be invoked only upon being satisfied that there has been a 'change in the circumstances' subsequent to the passing of the original order.

facts: A party (the respondent) filed an application under Section 25(2) of the Act to revoke a prior maintenance order dated 23.02.2015.
The respondent also sought a refund of the entire amount of maintenance that had already been paid under that order.
law: Section 25(2) of the Act allows a Magistrate to alter, modify, or revoke any order made under the Act if they are satisfied that there is a 'change in the circumstances'.
application: The Court held that the phrase 'change in the circumstances' is the essential condition for invoking Section 25(2).
The Court clarified that this change must occur *after* the original order was passed. It cannot be based on circumstances that existed prior to the original order.

The Court stated that any alteration, modification, or revocation under this section operates prospectively (ex post facto), meaning it applies from the date of the application or a later date as determined by the Magistrate.

It does not apply retrospectively. Therefore, an application under Section 25(2) cannot be used to set aside an order for a period before the application was filed, nor can it be used to claim a refund of maintenance already paid.

In this specific case, since the respondent's application sought to revoke the original order and get a refund for a prior period without demonstrating a subsequent change in circumstances, the Court found the application was not maintainable.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that a Magistrate's jurisdiction under Section 25(2) of the Act can only be invoked when the Magistrate is satisfied that there has been a 'change in the circumstances' that occurred subsequent to the passing of the original order.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the power under Section 25(2) of the Act to alter, modify, or revoke a maintenance order can be exercised retrospectively to set aside an order that has attained finality for a period prior to the filing of the application.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the High Court and the Appellate Court were wrong to remand the matter to the Magistrate for consideration of the respondent's application.
She contended that the respondent's application to set aside the original maintenance order of 23.02.2015 should be dismissed and the original order should be given effect.
respondent_arguments: The respondent filed an application under Section 25 of the Act with the specific prayer to set aside the original maintenance order dated 23.02.2015.
He argued that the Appellate Court and High Court were justified in remanding the matter to the Magistrate to consider his application for revocation of the order.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an application under Section 25(2) of the Act can be used to seek a refund of the maintenance amount already paid under the original order.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued for the dismissal of the respondent's application in its entirety, which implicitly opposes any prayer for a refund of maintenance already paid.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's application to set aside the original order from its date of passing implied a request for a refund of the amounts paid under that order.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the jurisdiction of a Magistrate under Section 25(2) of the Act can be invoked only upon being satisfied that there has been a 'change in the circumstances' subsequent to the passing of the original order.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's prayer to dismiss the respondent's application implies an argument that the necessary conditions to invoke the jurisdiction under Section 25(2), such as a change in circumstances, were not met.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that his application for revocation should be considered on its merits by the Magistrate, implying that the court had the jurisdiction to hear it.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A Magistrate may alter, modify, or revoke any order made under the Act if, upon an application from either the aggrieved person or the respondent, the Magistrate is satisfied that there has been a change in circumstances requiring such an action, and the reasons for the new order must be recorded in writing.
obiter: The Act is a piece of Civil Code which is applicable to every woman in India irrespective of her religious affiliation and/or social background for a more effective protection of her rights guaranteed under the Constitution and in order to protect women victims of domestic violence occurring in a domestic relationship.
